Great
grāt
adj. (large in magnitude, number, or dignity; rendering Hebrew gadol, rab, Greek megas)
From Saxon great, thick, coarse, large. The word runs the whole scale of Scripture: a great fish, a great multitude, a great commandment, and a great God — and the Bible never lets the smaller senses erode the greatest.

Biblical Definition

Great is one of the plainest words in the Authorized Version and one of the most theologically loaded, because Scripture applies it to God first and measures everything else against Him. Moses grounds Israel's obedience in it: “For the LORD your God is God of gods, and Lord of lords, a great God, a mighty, and a terrible, which regardeth not persons, nor taketh reward” (Deuteronomy 10:17). The Psalmist makes the greatness unmeasurable rather than merely large: “Great is the LORD, and greatly to be praised; and his greatness is unsearchable” (Psalm 145:3). This is the difference between a superlative and an attribute. A great mountain can be surveyed; a great God cannot, and the confession that His greatness is unsearchable is a confession of creaturely limit, not a compliment. From that fixed point the word orders lesser things. Our Lord ranks the commandments and calls the first one great (Matthew 22:38), which means greatness in the moral realm is assigned by God and not discovered by us. He is Himself named “that great shepherd of the sheep” (Hebrews 13:20), and the office is great because the blood by which He was raised is of infinite worth. Where men are called great in Scripture they are great derivatively — a great nation promised to Abraham, a great name given rather than seized — and where they grasp at greatness directly, as at Babel, the word turns against them.

Webster 1828 Definition

Large in bulk, number, or dignity; and by extension eminent, illustrious, of high rank. Scripture reserves the unqualified use for God, whose greatness Psalm 145 calls unsearchable, and assigns derived greatness to men and offices as He pleases.

expand to see more

GREAT, a. [Sax. great; D. groot; G. gross.] Large in bulk or dimensions; a term of comparison, denoting more magnitude or extension than something else, or beyond what is usual; as a great house; a great river.

2. Large in number; as a great many; a great multitude.

3. Expressing a large, extensive or unusual degree of any thing; as great fear; great love; great pain.

4. Eminent; distinguished; illustrious; as a great hero; a great statesman. Hence, of elevated rank or dignity; noble; magnanimous.

5. Chief; principal; of first importance; as the great commandment. Mat. 22. Applied to God, denoting the infinite excellence and majesty of the divine nature. Great is the Lord, and greatly to be praised. Ps. 145.

Key Scripture

Deuteronomy 10:17 — "For the LORD your God is God of gods, and Lord of lords, a great God, a mighty, and a terrible, which regardeth not persons, nor taketh reward:"

Psalm 145:3 — "Great is the LORD, and greatly to be praised; and his greatness is unsearchable."

Matthew 22:38 — "This is the first and great commandment."

Hebrews 13:20 — "Now the God of peace, that brought again from the dead our Lord Jesus, that great shepherd of the sheep, through the blood of the everlasting covenant,"

Modern Corruption

Greatness has been detached from God and reassigned to reach — audience, platform, influence — so that a man is called great for the size of the crowd he gathers rather than for the Master he serves.

expand to see more

The modern account of greatness is quantitative and self-referential: a great leader is one whose following is large, a great ministry is one whose numbers rise, a great life is one that leaves a measurable mark. Every one of those measures can be satisfied without God, and most of them are satisfied best by men who have no fear of Him. Scripture does not merely add a religious qualifier to this scale; it inverts it. “Whosoever will be great among you, let him be your minister” sets the standard where no crowd can see it, and the Lord who said it washed feet. The reversal is not a paradox for devotional effect. It follows from Deuteronomy 10:17: the great God regardeth not persons, which means the very thing that makes a man great in the world's reckoning — that he is a person of consequence, worth regarding — is precisely what God does not weigh.

The second corruption is subtler and works inside the church. Because great is a comparative word, it can be applied to God in a way that only means bigger than the rest, and a God who is merely the largest item in the universe is still an item in it. Psalm 145:3 forbids this: His greatness is unsearchable, not simply unmatched. Recover that and worship changes character. Praise is no longer the awarding of a superlative by a creature competent to judge the field; it is the confession of a greatness that exceeds the instrument measuring it. That is why the same verse pairs greatness with praise and then admits defeat — greatly to be praised, and still unsearchable. The proper end of the word is not flattery but silence, and then obedience.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew gadol (great, large, elder) and rab (many, much, chief); Greek megas (great in any dimension), polys (much, many), and the comparative meizon our Lord uses to rank greatness in the kingdom.

expand to see more

Hebrew gadol (H1419) — great, large, elder; the word in “a great God” (Deuteronomy 10:17) and “Great is the LORD” (Psalm 145:3).

Hebrew gadal (H1431) — to grow, become great, magnify; the verb behind Abraham's promised great name and behind magnifying the LORD.

Hebrew rab (H7227) — much, many, great in number or rank; often rendered great of a multitude or of a chief officer.

Greek megas (G3173) — great in magnitude, degree, or dignity; the word in “the first and great commandment” (Matthew 22:38).

Greek meizon (G3187) — greater, the comparative of megas; the term in the disciples' dispute over who should be greatest.

Usage

"“A great God, a mighty, and a terrible” — greatness named together with power and holy dread, not with popularity."

"“His greatness is unsearchable” — the attribute exceeds the creature measuring it."

"“That great shepherd of the sheep” — the office is great because of the blood that purchased it."
